lesson.title: The Would-World & Subjunctive Preview
lesson.subtitle: me gustaría, podrías, and the opposite-vowel subjunctive after wishes

hook.title: Two Moods Beyond Plain Fact: The Conditional (-ía) & The Subjunctive
hook.content: First, the **Conditional ('would')**: take ANY full infinitive verb (gustar, hablar, comer, vivir) and glue **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían** straight onto the end without removing -ar/-er/-ir! Thus me gusta ('it pleases me / I like') becomes **me gustaría** ('it would please me' = **'I would like'**): Me gustaría reservar una mesa! Second, the **Subjunctive**: when you want, hope, or say it's important that SOMEONE ELSE do something (Quiero que tú..., Es importante que..., Ojalá...), Spanish switches the verb's theme vowel to the **OPPOSITE vowel**: -ar verbs switch from -a to **-e** (hablas → **hables**, hable), and -er/-ir verbs switch from -e/-i to **-a** (comes → **comas**, tengas, viva)!

pattern.title: When to Use Infinitive vs Subjunctive: Same Person vs Two People!
pattern.content:
• **One person** ('I want to speak'): Quiero hablar (simple infinitive!).
• **Two people connected by 'que'** ('I want YOU to speak' = 'I want that you speak'): **Quiero que hables** (opposite-vowel subjunctive!)!
pattern.linguist_note: The Romance conditional fused the Latin infinitive with the imperfect of habēre (gustāre + habēbam → gustaría), which is why -ía stays attached to the whole infinitive!
pattern.trap_note: Never say *Quiero tú hablar (copying English 'I want you to speak'). Whenever the subject changes after querer, Spanish requires que + subjunctive: Quiero que hables!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: I would like (it would please me: gustar + -ía)
could you / I could (polite conditional of poder)
that you speak (-ar flips to opposite vowel -e!)
that you eat (-er flips to opposite vowel -a!)

exercises.target_answer: me gustaría, podrías / podría, que hables, que comas, ojalá
exercises.meaning: I would like (it would please me: gustar + -ía), could you / I could (polite conditional of poder), that you speak (-ar flips to opposite vowel -e!), that you eat (-er flips to opposite vowel -a!), hopefully / God willing (always triggers subjunctive!)
exercises.explanation: Conditional = full infinitive + -ía; Subjunctive = opposite ending vowel (-ar → -e, -er/-ir → -a).

exercises.prompt: Build 'would like / would please' by gluing the conditional ending '-ía' onto the full infinitive 'gustar':
How does Spanish express 'I want you to speak Spanish' (literally 'I want that you speak Spanish')?
exercises.meaning: I want you to speak Spanish
exercises.explanation: After Quiero que..., the second verb switches its -ar ending (-as) to the opposite vowel (-es): que hables!

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I would like to reserve a table'
exercises.meaning: I would like to reserve a table
exercises.explanation: Me gustaría ('I would like') + reservar una mesa.

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'Quiero que hables conmigo'?
exercises.natural: I want you to speak with me
options: You want that I speak with me
I want to speak with you
I want you to speak with me
exercises.meaning: I want you to speak with me (literal Spanish blueprint: I-want that you-speak(subj.) with-me)
exercises.explanation: English uses an object + infinitive ('want you to speak'); Spanish uses 'Quiero que + subjunctive' ('I-want that you-speak').

summary.outcome: Form the polite conditional (me gustaría, podría) and the opposite-vowel subjunctive after quiero que / es importante que.

use_example.german: Me gustaría reservar una mesa y quiero que hables con mi amigo.
use_example.english: I would like to reserve a table and I want you to speak with my friend.

summary.takeaway: Conditional = infinitive + -ía; Subjunctive = flip -ar to -e and -er/-ir to -a after que.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2601] The Conditional of Politeness): soften requests with me gustaría and ¿podrías...?

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'I would like a coffee, please'
twist.target_answer: Me gustaría un café por favor
twist.explanation: Me gustaría un café, por favor.

foreshadow.line: You just unlocked the Deep Engine Gate! In Topic 27, we enter Phase 5 (Synthesis) by decoding the three historical sound shifts that unlock hundreds of deep Spanish roots: f-→h-, -ct-→-ch-, and pl-/cl-→ll-!

payoff.text: Me gusta ('I like') from Topic 25 turns effortlessly into Me gustaría ('I would like') simply by adding -ía to gustar!

gustaría.english_cognate: would please (me gustaría: I would like)
gustaría.english_meaning: would please (conditional: me gustaría = I would like)
gustaría.context_translation: I would like to reserve a table.
gustaría.etymology_derivation: Every Spanish conditional simply glues -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían onto the whole infinitive!

ojalá.english_meaning: hopefully, I hope that, if only (always triggers subjunctive!)
ojalá.context_translation: I hope you have a great day!
ojalá.etymology_derivation: Direct Arabic inheritance in Spanish; always triggers the subjunctive mood (tengas, venga, sea)!

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.

tener.etymology_derivation: Latin tenēre ('to hold'). While other tongues used 'have' (like French avoir), Spanish promoted 'hold' (tener) to main possession.

reservar.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.

hablar.english_meaning: to speak, to talk (hablo: I speak)
hablar.etymology_derivation: Latin fabulārī (to converse, tell stories — English fable and fabulous) shifted initial f- to silent h-: hablar!

comer.etymology_derivation: Latin com- ('completely') + edere ('to eat', cousin of English edible and eat).

mesa.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.
mesa.etymology_derivation: Latin mēnsa ('table') gave Spanish la mesa — which English borrowed in the American Southwest for a flat-topped 'table' mountain!

importante.etymology_derivation: Adjectives ending in -e do not change for gender: el punto importante, la idea importante.

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
